newsitem.title: FRANCE: French report urges Airbus A3XX launch aid.
newsitem.headline: French report urges Airbus A3XX launch aid.

text.p: A French senator urged the government on Tuesday to use the full range of financing tools to launch a planned Airbus super-jumbo to keep Europe competitive with the United States.

Yvon Collin, author of a Senate finance committee report on public support for the commercial aircraft industry, said Europe's Airbus Industrie consortium needed to attack the monopoly held by Boeing Co's 747 jumbo in the high-capacity market.
"The necessary development of the A3XX launches a major challenge to the GIE (Groupement Interet Economique) and the governments concerned," Collin told journalists.

The four-nation Airbus consortium is made up as a GIE, or partnership, between French state-owned Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (Casa) of Spain.
Last week, U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin said it was merging with Northrop Grumman in an $11.6 billion deal.
The U.S. Federal Trade Commission, meanwhile, approved a merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas to create a colossus with $48 billion in sales in space, military and civil aviation.

The Collin report also called for the merger of Aerospatiale and combat plane maker Dassault Aviation to create a strong French national champion and as a means to double Aerospatiale's capital base to 10 billion francs ($1.7 billion).
But Aerospatiale needed a further recapitalisation to make it competitive, it said.
Industry forecasts for passenger jets estimate that the market will grow by $55 billion a year until 2015, justifying the state's investment in this strategic industry, Collin said.

Future demand for planes seating 400-plus passengers will account for $254.1 billion, or 22.7 percent, of the total aircraft market, according to Boeing statistics reproduced in the report. Airbus needs the A3XX 500-seater to stay in the race, or face annihilation, he said.

The profit margin on a 747 was $15-30 million and allowed Boeing to offer a complete product range to airlines. Airbus could not allow itself to be excluded from essentially a quarter of the world market, Collin said.

Given the strategic value of the industry, the French government needed to use the system of repayable launch aid and fund research and development to the full permissible level. It should also recapitalise Aerospatiale and aero-engine maker Snecma.

Under a 1992 bilateral agreement between the United States and the European Union, governments can fund up to 33 percent of programme costs through launch aid and finance research and development up to three percent of a company's annual turnover.
But France had let launch aid slip to 726 million francs in 1997, representing a third of the amount paid out in 1986, the report said.
Aerospatiale actually faces a net outflow this year as it repays two billion francs from previous launch aid and will receive only 312 million francs.

In contrast to the lukewarm financial support of the French authorities, the report pointed to $29 billion in Pentagon research funding for the U.S. industry and military orders which indirectly support the civil side.

The U.S. industry also enjoys the support of President Bill Clinton and the Washington political machine, whereas French state-owned firms can only draw on shared responsibility between the transport and defence ministries, with a disproportionately large voice for the latter, even in commercial projects.
The report will go President Jacques Chirac, Prime Minister Lionel Jospin and Transport Minister Jean-Claude Gayssot. ($ = 5.907 French Francs)
